<description>
This PR keeps the windowed table from #36327 but accumulate the selected entries in integer Jacobian coordinates, needing a single modular inversion per multiplication instead of one full affine FE addition per window. On my machine, it speeds up feature_taproot.py  by ~38% (M1 Pro). Also, adds a unit test cross-checking against the generic GE.mul.
</description>

[2026-11-21] c:7060342795 comment by theStack (member):
Concept ACK

My initial gut feeling reaction to this PR was that introducing another coordinate system merely for speeding up a single functional test (even if it's a very important one) might be a bit over the top, but given the concrete [motivation](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36896#issuecomment-6980935327) for speeding up the mutation testing pipeline, it seems worth it for the additional complexity. I think though the stated "ease of understanding" design goal of the FE/GE classes introduced in #26222 is very valuable and should still be kept, and I'd thus likely not be in favor of any future optimizations outside of `FastGEMul` (where one could argue that the name already implies that adding some complexity for speed is okay) that sacrifice simplicity/readability.

The idea of using [projective instead of Jacobian coordinates](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36896#issuecomment-6975861858) sounds very appealing to me, happy to review that.

I think in addition to the very good reasons already mentioned against using libsecp256k1 directly (potential maintenance burden, loss of test diversity, lack of low-level primitives) there another very practical one: it also doesn't provide the needed functionality on a higher-level: e.g. the taproot signing function in the test framework has options for intentionally creating invalid signatures [with flipped R and P signs](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/004cfb21a51db563b92cde968f249086ef58df7c/test/functional/test_framework/key.py#L267), which `feature_taproot.py` uses. (This is by the way also one of the technical blockers for subtree-ing secp256k1lab, see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34287). So we'd need to keep the Python ECC implementation anyways, and have some functions which sometimes use the bindings, sometimes not, which I think would get quite confusing.
</new_statements>
